Iran-Contra. The scandal that revealed how senior government officials could secretly bypass Congress and the law itself to pursue their own foreign policy.

Between 1985 and 1987, senior officials in the Reagan administration were negotiating in secret. National Security Advisor John Poindexter and National Security Council aide Oliver North were the key players. They were facilitating arms sales to Iran, something that violated the law.

The United States had placed an embargo on Iran after the 1979 revolution. It was illegal to sell weapons there. But the Reagan administration claimed they were seeking better relations with Iranian moderates. That was the cover story. In reality, they were sending weapons.

Approximately thirty million dollars in proceeds came from these arms sales. And that money went somewhere crucial. It was funneled illegally to the Contras. These were right-wing guerrilla fighters opposing Nicaragua's Sandinista government.

But Congress had explicitly forbidden military aid to the Contras. The Boland Amendment, passed in 1982 and renewed through 1987, made military support illegal. The administration knew this. They did it anyway. They circumvented a constitutional constraint through classified operations that only a handful of people knew about.

Oliver North admitted to destroying evidence and obstructing Congress. John Poindexter misled Congress during testimony. A special prosecutor was appointed in 1986, and multiple officials were indicted. Most of them received presidential pardons in December 1992, just days before President Reagan left office. Reagan essentially cleaned house for everyone involved.

The scandal raised urgent and fundamental questions. How much power should the executive branch have in foreign policy? Can Congress actually enforce its will on military matters? What does the rule of law mean when officials can break it and face no real consequences?

Ronald Reagan was the president under whose administration the scheme was authorized. Oliver North orchestrated the operation and destroyed evidence. John Poindexter, as National Security Advisor, approved the diversion of funds. The scandal was rooted in the broader Nicaragua conflict, where America was fighting the Sandinista government, and it was driven by the Iran-Iraq War, which gave the administration an excuse to engage with Iran at all.
